Compare {{cog|sco|kut}}, {{m|sco|kit|t=to cut}}); also akin to Middle {{cog|sv|kotta|t=to cut or carve with a knife}} (compare dialectal {{cog|sv|kåta}}, {{m|sv|kuta|t=to cut or chip with a knife}}, {{cog|sv|kuta}}, {{m|sv|kytti|t=a knife}}), {{cog|nb|kutte|t=to cut}}, {{cog|nn|kutte|t=to cut}}, {{cog|is|kuta|t=to cut with a knife}}, {{cog|non|kuti|t=small knife}}, {{cog|no|kyttel}}, {{m|no|kytel}}, {{m|no|kjutul|t=pointed slip of wood used to strip bark}}. {{displaced|enm|snithen}} (from {{m|ang|snīþan}}), still attested in dialectal {{m|en|snithe}} and {{m|en|snead}}. See {{m|en|snide}}.

The adjective sense of "drunk" (now rare and now usually used in the originally humorous derivative form of {{m|en|half-cut}}) dates from the 17th century, from {{m|en||cut in the leg}} or {{m|en||to have cut your leg}}, a {{lg|euphemism}} for being very drunk.
